notes.meaning: The family heads of the Levites, the tribe chosen to serve God, came to Joshua, Eleazar the high priest, and the tribal leaders at Shiloh. They reminded the leaders that the Lord had told Moses to give them towns to live in and open fields for their animals. The Levites waited patiently until every other tribe received land before asking for what God had promised. God's people can trust his promises even when they have to wait their turn.

differ.view: The other tribes had grown careless and neglected the Levites until the Levites stepped forward to plead their own case.
The Levites were not forgotten; their request simply came in proper order after the other tribes knew what territory they had to share.

notes.meaning: The people of Israel gladly obeyed the Lord's command and gave the Levites specific towns and pastures out of their own tribal lands. God did not give the Levites a large province of their own, so the other tribes shared what they had received. In this way, every tribe helped support the workers who led them in worship.

The first lot was drawn for the Kohathite clan, beginning with the family of Aaron the priest. A lot was a method like drawing stones to let God reveal his choice. Aaron's descendants received thirteen cities from the southern tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin. Long before the temple was built in Jerusalem, God placed the priests close to where they would later serve.

The rest of the Kohathite families, who were Levite assistants rather than priests, received ten cities by lot. These towns were taken from the territories of Ephraim, Dan, and the western half-tribe of Manasseh. This placed these families in central Canaan, right next to their priestly relatives.

The families descended from Gershon received thirteen cities by lot from the northern tribes. Their towns were spread across Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan, east of the Jordan River. Scattering them among the northern tribes helped teach God's word to people living far from the main worship tent.

The families of Merari received twelve cities from the lands of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun. Reuben and Gad lived east of the Jordan River, while Zebulun was settled in the north. This completed the total of forty-eight towns that God had told Moses to provide for the Levites.

Israel distributed these cities and pasturelands by lot, just as the Lord had ordered through Moses. The pastureland was grazing ground that stretched out around each town wall so the Levites could feed their cattle and sheep. Having Levites in every region meant all the tribes had spiritual teachers living right near them.

The tribes of Judah and Simeon named the specific cities assigned to Aaron's priestly family. The priests received the very first lot because of their sacred calling to offer sacrifices and lead Israel in worship. Simeon is named alongside Judah because Simeon's towns were located inside Judah's larger territory.

The leaders gave the priests Kiriath-arba, also called Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, along with its grazing lands. The city got its ancient name from Arba, a great ruler among the giant Anakim who used to live there. Hebron was an important town and later became the place where David first ruled as king.

differ.view: The Levites were the true owners and proprietors of the cities given to them, not merely guest tenants.
The Levites held rights only to certain houses and pasture, while other Israelites continued to live in and share the cities.

notes.meaning: The Levites received the town of Hebron and the pastures right outside it, but Caleb kept the surrounding farms and villages. Caleb had conquered this area in faith and willingly shared the city itself with God's ministers while keeping his own family inheritance. Generous people are glad to share their property to support the work of God.

notes.meaning: The priests received Hebron, which had already been designated as a city of refuge, along with the town of Libnah. A city of refuge was a safe place where someone who killed another person by accident could run to escape revenge. Placing these safe towns in the hands of the priests ensured that fair and godly leaders handled the cases.

The list of priestly cities continues with Jattir, Eshtemoa, Holon, Debir, Ain, Juttah, and Beth-shemesh. In all, nine towns and their grazing lands came from the tribes of Judah and Simeon. Beth-shemesh later became well known as the town where the ark of the covenant was returned by the Philistines.

From the small tribe of Benjamin, the priests were given four cities: Gibeon, Geba, Anathoth, and Almon, along with their pasturelands. Anathoth later became famous as the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah. Benjamin gave generously from its small territory so the Lord's priests could live close to where the tabernacle would serve.

In all, thirteen cities with their pasturelands were assigned to the priests from Aaron's family. There were only a few priests alive at that time, but God gave them enough room for their families to grow over the centuries. God thoughtfully plans ahead to meet the future needs of his servants.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that this list reflects a much later period in Israel's history, because several of these towns were not fully occupied by Israel in Joshua's day.

notes.meaning: The remaining families of the Kohathite clan, who were Levites but not priests, were allotted their towns from the tribe of Ephraim. These families included the descendants of Moses and Aaron's relatives. God took care of these supporting workers just as faithfully as he provided for the priests.

Ephraim gave these Levites four towns: Shechem in the hill country, Gezer, Kibzaim, and Beth-horon, along with their pasturelands. Shechem was located in the mountains where it could be seen from far away, making it easy to find as a city of refuge for accidental killers. These towns settled Levite families right in central Israel where they could help and instruct their neighbors.
